To: Executive Supply Chain Leadership  
From: Sustainability & Logistics Director  
Subject: Balancing Transportation Cost and Carbon Impact Across Our Warehouse-to-Store Network  
Date:

Context
Our distribution network ships finished goods from multiple warehouses to stores across the region. Each potential shipping route has two performance metrics: a monetary cost per unit and a carbon emission rate per unit. In practice, these metrics often move in opposite directions—many of the lowest-cost lanes also have higher emissions. We need a network-wide plan that balances financial discipline with our sustainability commitments while maintaining reliable service to every store.

Operational Rules and Realities
- Route activation costs: Opening any shipping lane requires an upfront, one-time setup charge (e.g., contract fees, compliance documentation, dock scheduling). A lane is either active or not. If active, the setup cost is incurred regardless of the volume we move on that lane.
- Minimum order quantities: Once a lane is activated, we must ship at least a defined minimum volume on that lane to justify transportation and handling—partial loads are not accepted by carriers or docks.
- Supplier limits per store: To manage receiving dock capacity, scheduling, and vendor administration, each store can receive deliveries from at most a defined number of warehouses.

Supply and Service Boundaries
- Warehouse capacity: Each warehouse has a finite inventory available to ship. Our plan must not exceed these available units.
- Store service levels: Each store has a minimum demand requirement that must be met within the planning horizon. Stockouts are not acceptable.

Management Priority: Cost vs. Emissions
Leadership has set explicit importance weights for cost and emissions. These weights reflect a pragmatic balance: cost control remains paramount, while carbon reduction is a meaningful, measurable priority. To reflect this guidance, our evaluation will combine:
- Variable shipping cost, scaled by the cost importance weight.
- Total route emissions, scaled by the emissions importance weight.
- Route setup charges for any activated lanes, added in full (not weighted).

Goal and Decision Framework
We will recommend which routes to activate and how much to ship on each active route to achieve the best overall outcome under our real-world rules. The plan will:
- Respect warehouse inventory limits and fulfill each store’s minimum demand.
- Activate a route only if we are prepared to pay the setup charge and ship at least the minimum order quantity on that route.
- Limit each store’s inbound deliveries to the allowed number of supplying warehouses.
- Minimize the blended total of (weighted variable shipping cost) plus (weighted emissions) plus (full setup costs).

Deliverables and Next Steps
- Proposed route activation list and shipment allocations by warehouse–store lane, with confirmation that all operational rules are satisfied.
- Sensitivity views showing how the plan shifts if leadership adjusts the relative importance of cost and emissions or modifies the supplier limit or minimum order thresholds.
- Implementation checklist covering carrier contracting, dock scheduling, and emissions reporting.
